findings.problem: The stock-shortage remainder timeframe is stated only as 'Within 72 hours', with no anchor, while the adjacent request-based emergency-oral entry timing_deadlines[5] is anchored 'No later than 72 hours after issue'.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.13(a) runs its 72-hour period from the first partial filling, whereas 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(2) runs its emergency-oral 72-hour period from issuance of the prescription. The two anchors can fall days apart. Presenting one anchored and one unanchored 72-hour deadline side by side invites the reader to assume a common anchor, which defeats the section's own learning objective of choosing the correct deadline by pathway.

findings.problem: Massachusetts is characterized only as adding 'same-pharmacy, patient-record, and issue-date conditions' to a permissive federal option. The section never states that M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) makes partial dispensing mandatory on patient request, nor that s. 22(c) requires a Schedule II opioid prescription to carry a notation informing the patient of that right.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.13(b) is permissive ('may be partially filled'). M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) is mandatory: a pharmacist filling a Schedule II prescription SHALL, if requested by the patient, dispense the substance in a lesser quantity than indicated on the prescription. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) reinforces this by requiring the prescription itself to notify the patient of the right. The mandatory duty, not the recordkeeping conditions, is the principal Massachusetts-versus-federal divergence for this topic; a reader relying on this element could conclude the pharmacist retains discretion to refuse.

findings.problem: The federal state-law condition is paraphrased as partial filling operating 'only where state law permits' and 'and state law permits it'.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(1)(i) states the condition as 'It is not prohibited by State law.' Converting a not-prohibited condition into an affirmative-permission condition inverts the default for a jurisdiction whose law is silent.

findings.problem: Emergency oral dispensing is described as following 'reasonable prescriber identification' without stating the condition that triggers that duty.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(3) imposes the reasonable-effort identification duty only if the prescribing individual practitioner is not known to the pharmacist. Stating it unconditionally overstates the duty's scope.

results.summary: Every cited federal and Massachusetts proposition was independently confirmed against current primary authority, including the difficult point that the Massachusetts five-day initial partial-dispensing limit reaches only prescriptions filled under s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2). Three defects prevent an exact-current-hash KEEP: an unanchored 72-hour stock-shortage deadline presented beside an anchored 72-hour emergency-oral deadline, an ma_vs_federal element that omits the mandatory Massachusetts partial-dispensing duty and its s. 22(c) prescription notation, and a not-prohibited-versus-permitted paraphrase drift. All are additive or wording-level repairs; no existing legal proposition was found false.

findings.problem: The section covers Schedule III-V transfers without stating the controlling federal limit that transfer of Schedule III, IV or V prescription information for refill purposes is permissible between pharmacies on a one-time basis only, absent a shared real-time online database. 21 CFR 1306.25 is not among the section's rule dependencies.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.25(a) is the principal federal constraint on the exact transaction this section teaches. ma_vs_federal[1] tells the reader that the federal five-refill and six-month limits remain operative when Massachusetts transfer rules are applied, which implies those are the federal limits that survive a transfer. A reader applying the mandatory transfer duty in 247 CMR 9.14(1) to a Schedule IV prescription already transferred once would reach an unlawful result.

findings.problem: Massachusetts follow-up timing for an oral Schedule III-V prescription is presented solely as 'Within 7 days or shorter federal period' under the s. 18(c) out-of-state pathway. The section does not surface the other Massachusetts periods that reach the same oral controlled-substance transaction.
findings.rationale: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) requires the practitioner to cause an electronic prescription to be delivered within 2 days, and permits a written prescription within not more than 7 days only where the practitioner holds a s. 23(h) exception. 105 CMR 721.070(B) sets a separate period of not more than seven BUSINESS days for an oral Schedule II-V prescription issued under an ePrescribing exception. A single unqualified seven-day figure conceals a 2-day, 7-day and 7-business-day distinction that is directly testable.

findings.problem: By naming only the federal five-refill and six-month limits as the federal constraints that remain operative during a Massachusetts transfer, the element implies the federal transfer regime imposes nothing further.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.25 imposes the one-time transfer limit and detailed pharmacist-to-pharmacist recording duties that also remain operative. The enumeration reads as exhaustive and is not.

findings.problem: The section's only role duty assigns the transfer obligation to the 'Receiving pharmacy'.
findings.rationale: 247 CMR 9.14(1) places the mandatory duty on the pharmacy holding the prescription: a pharmacy shall transfer a prescription to another pharmacy, at the request of a patient or the patient's agent, in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy. 247 CMR 9.14(2) separately permits a pharmacy to act as the patient's agent. Naming only the receiving pharmacy leaves the mandatory actor unstated.

results.summary: The Massachusetts material is exceptionally precise and was confirmed verbatim, including the 247 CMR 9.04(15) exclusion list that reaches 9.04(13), the 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) one-year Schedule VI remaining-refill transfer bar, and the correct reading that the s. 18(c) seven-day period governs practitioner delivery rather than pharmacist recording. Exact-current-hash KEEP is nevertheless withheld because the federal one-time transfer limit in 21 CFR 1306.25 is absent from a section whose declared scope is Schedule III-V refills and transfers, and because the Massachusetts oral follow-up timing is reduced to a single unqualified seven-day figure. The repair is additive and requires one new canonical rule dependency.

findings.location: topic 'Schedule VI prescription lifecycle'; learning_objectives[2]; timing_deadlines[1]; common_traps[3]
findings.problem: The section states no general validity limit for a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription. It carries only the 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) one-year limit on transferring a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills, and common_traps[3] expressly warns the reader not to restate that rule as a universal window.
findings.rationale: 247 CMR 9.04(12) provides that a prescription for a Schedule VI medication is valid for one year from the date of issue and that a licensee may not refill a Schedule VI prescription after one year. It further permits the pharmacist, in professional judgment, to dispense a quantity not exceeding a 14-day supply or the smallest available unit-of-use package where the prescription has expired or has no remaining refills and prescriber authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner. Omitting the controlling validity rule while warning against generalizing the transfer rule can leave the reader believing no general one-year limit exists.

findings.problem: The section presents Schedule VI purely as a classification that withholds consequences, with no counterweight for Schedule VI substances designated as Additional Drugs.
findings.rationale: 105 CMR 700.001 defines an Additional Drug as a controlled substance in Schedule VI that the Department determines carries a bona fide potential for abuse, and 105 CMR 700.012 governs Prescription Monitoring Program obligations. 247 CMR 9.04(14)(b) requires a Customer Identifier for a prescription for a controlled substance in Schedules II through V or a controlled substance classified as an additional drug in accordance with 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1). A reader could conclude Schedule VI never triggers identification or monitoring-program obligations.

findings.problem: A candidate using this section cannot answer the most basic Schedule VI lifecycle question, namely how long the prescription remains valid and what may be dispensed once it lapses.
findings.rationale: The section's declared topic is the Schedule VI prescription lifecycle and its second learning objective covers validity, documentation, dispensing and transfer, yet validity and the expired-prescription dispensing allowance in 247 CMR 9.04(12) are absent.

results.summary: Every proposition the section does assert was confirmed verbatim against current authority: 105 CMR 700.002(F) defines Schedule VI as all prescription drugs not included in any other schedule established by the Commissioner; 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9) excepts Schedule VI prescriptions from the electronic-prescribing mandate; 105 CMR 721.070(C) relieves the pharmacist of verifying that an exception applies; and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) expressly does not reach Schedule VI. KEEP is withheld because the section omits 247 CMR 9.04(12), the controlling Schedule VI validity and expired-prescription rule, and gives no counterweight for Schedule VI Additional Drugs. Nothing asserted is false; the defects are omissions inside the section's own declared scope.

findings.problem: The section's headline federal proposition is that patient-requested Schedule II partial filling is 'conditioned on state law permitting the partial fill', repeated in decision_logic[2] as federal law permitting the partial fill where state law allows it.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(1)(i) conditions the partial fill on its being 'not prohibited by State law'. In a module whose declared purpose is precision about federal-state interaction, restating a not-prohibited condition as an affirmative-permission condition inverts the default and is the one paraphrase this section can least afford to get wrong.

findings.problem: The only Schedule II timing entry gives an unqualified 'No later than 30 days after issue' for the patient-requested remainder, omitting both the federal emergency-oral variant and the Massachusetts five-day initial-dispensing limit.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(2) requires the remainder of a partially filled emergency oral Schedule II prescription to be filled not later than 72 hours after issuance rather than 30 days. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) requires the initial partial dispensing of a prescription filled pursuant to s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2) to occur not more than five days after the issue date. Both are exactly the shorter controlling limits this module's method is meant to surface, and both are carried by the section's own rule dependencies.

findings.problem: The consequence field states only that both federal and Massachusetts pathway limits must be satisfied, without identifying which limit is shorter in any concrete pathway.
findings.rationale: The interaction skill being taught is selecting the controlling limit. Stating that both apply, without the 72-hour and five-day variants, leaves the reader with a single number to apply.

results.summary: The section's scope-matching method is sound and its Massachusetts Schedule V facility-scope treatment is precise: 247 CMR 9.04(15) was confirmed verbatim to exclude institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 247 CMR 9.04(13). KEEP is withheld because the module's headline federal proposition restates the 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(1)(i) not-prohibited condition as an affirmative state-permission condition, and because its single Schedule II timing entry omits the 72-hour emergency-oral variant and the Massachusetts five-day initial-dispensing limit that the interaction method exists to surface.
